text: Can a mosquito drink until she bursts?
Weirdly, yes. In a lab, it really happened.
So here's what bugs me: why doesn't every mosquito pop?
First clue: one tiny nerve.
A nerve? Please, suspect number one is muscles.
They say flex while she's drinking, and your blood pressure pumps her till she pops.
I even bought muscle sleeves. Case closed.
Not so fast, detective; this case is wide open.
Later, he's still wearing the sleeves, because of course he is.
And a mosquito lands on his arm, all on her own.
Shh, it's Operation Flex. Any second now…
She drinks her fill, then tiptoes off like nothing happened.
…Did my muscles do anything? Not a thing, unless you count that itchy bump.
He took that bite for the team, so you don't have to.
Honestly, I flexed at mosquitoes for years.
But there's no good evidence it works, and entomologists call it a myth.
A myth?! I bought sleeves!
She isn't getting pumped up by your blood pressure.
She sucks it up herself, with little pumps in her head.
So she's the pump… and I'm the juice box.
So flexing won't pop her. But in that lab, something did.
She's tiny, so how much can she even fit?
In a couple of minutes, she can drink a meal heavier than she is.
The dinner weighs more than the diner?
For you, that's like drinking… a whole second you.
Then suspect number two: her belly fills up like a water balloon, so she stops. Case closed.
Reopened. Her belly expands like an accordion, making room as she drinks.
And some mosquitoes do something stranger: they pee while still drinking. At the table?!
They squeeze out water to pack in more of the good stuff.
I had to read that twice. Worst dinner guest ever.
So she quits long before she runs out of room.
Then who tells her to stop? Her stomach, obviously.
Close: as her belly stretches, sensors along it call her brain on one nerve line.
Ring ring, it's Belly calling Brain: we're full!
And the brain says: stop. That line is the one tiny nerve I promised you.
So what happens if that line goes dead? Only one way to find out.
Easy there; a scientist already tried it in a lab, back in 1969.
He cut that exact line, between a mosquito's belly and her brain.
One cut beat my whole arm?
Same belly, same stretching, but the call never gets through.
A normal meal is over in about two minutes.
These kept going… three minutes… four… five. Somebody stop her!
They drank over four times a normal meal.
And many of them kept drinking until their bellies burst.
…I did not need that picture in my head.
So, can a mosquito drink until she bursts?
Yes, if the call to stop never comes.
So she stops when she gets the call… not when she's out of room.
Wait… the one that bit me. Is she coming back for seconds tonight?
Let's ask the one from earlier, resting on the table.
The detective, being the detective, leans in and flexes in her face. She turns away.
She's… ignoring me. She is, and honestly, I respect it.
After a full meal, she can lose interest in people for days, until she lays her eggs.
Easy: her belly just keeps calling "full" for days. Case closed.
Reopened, and this part surprised me.
That days-long feeling isn't the phone line; it's chemical.
Like a sticky note that says: already ate?
…Could somebody forge that note? Somebody did.
In 2019, scientists grabbed a diet drug made for humans.
They fed it to mosquitoes in a meal with no blood at all.
You put a mosquito on a diet?
The mosquitoes acted like they'd already eaten, and lost interest in people for about two days.
They forged the note… beautiful. Where do I buy it?
It was a lab test, not a bug spray. Wallet away, detective.
Back at his desk, one thing is still pumped up.
I'd like to return these muscles. Reason for the return?
Case closed… my biceps were not involved.
